summary: At just 47 square miles — smaller than many suburban townships — San Francisco packs 827,000 residents into one of the most vertically dramatic urban landscapes in the country, where a ten-minute walk can mean a 300-foot elevation change and a completely different microclimate. That density of 17,570 people per square mile fuels a genuinely walkable, transit-rich city: BART, Muni buses, cable cars, and streetcars form a web that makes car-free living plausible, and Golden Gate Park stretches over a thousand acres from the Haight to Ocean Beach. The median household income of $141,446 sounds formidable until you set it against a median home price of $1,380,500 — a price-to-income ratio near 9.8, meaning even well-compensated households face steep math on a purchase; median rent at $2,419 consumes roughly 20% of that median gross income, which is manageable but tightens fast at lower earnings. The job center gravity here is real: tech, biotech, healthcare (anchored by UCSF), and financial services mean many residents commute within the city limits or a short BART hop south. Property crime runs high at 4,620 per 100,000 — motor vehicle theft alone at 658 per 100,000 is a standout line item worth studying before deciding where and how to park. Summer highs average only 63°F with heavy fog rolling through the western half while the eastern neighborhoods sit in sun, a split so pronounced that packing a jacket for a crosstown errand is year-round habit. San Francisco is a city where the median income qualifies as comfortable for renting and strained for buying — a tension that defines daily life as much as the fog.
